chapters.title: Chapter 4: Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis

lessons.title: Building a Stress Testing Framework for a Trading Book

children.text: This course has covered VaR through three methods, Expected Shortfall, backtesting, and now historical, hypothetical, and sensitivity-based stress testing. Individually, each is a technique. Run once and filed away, none of them protects anyone. A stress testing framework is what turns these individual techniques into an operating discipline, something a desk actually runs on a schedule, escalates when it breaches, and keeps current as markets change.

body.label: Stress Testing Framework
body.value: A recurring, governed process for running, reviewing, and acting on scenario and sensitivity results, not a one-time analysis
body.context: The difference between a framework and a technique is what happens after the number comes out.

children.text: The Five Components of a Working Framework

body.caption: What turns individual stress tests into a real framework

cells: A maintained set of historical scenarios (Chapter 4, Lesson 2) and hypothetical scenarios (Lesson 3), reviewed and refreshed as new vulnerabilities emerge
How often each tool runs, VaR typically daily, formal stress scenarios typically weekly or monthly, ad hoc sensitivity grids whenever a new position type is added
Explicit rules on how much loss any single scenario is allowed to imply, separate from routine VaR-based position limits
Who reviews results, and what specifically triggers a risk committee conversation versus a routine log entry
Checking whether the scenario library itself is still relevant, the same spirit as backtesting, applied to the stress testing process rather than the VaR model

children.text: Putting It All Together: One Portfolio, Every Tool From This Course
A single consolidated risk dashboard for the Nifty-and-import-payable-and-bond portfolio used across this course pulls together every technique into one page.

body.caption: Consolidated risk dashboard, drawing on figures computed across this course

cells: Worst historical stress scenario (GFC, full portfolio)
Worst two-factor sensitivity grid cell (equity and FX only)

body.text: Look at the gap between the first row and the rest. A daily 99% VaR of Rs 1,39,560 and a GFC-scenario loss of Rs 42,75,000 describe the same portfolio, roughly a 30-fold difference. This is the entire thesis of this course in one table: VaR tells you what an ordinary bad day looks like, and it does that job well, but it was never built to warn you about a crisis, that is stress testing's job, and no framework is complete without both running side by side.

children.text: Setting Limits from Stress Results, Not Just VaR

A stress-test-based limit is a separate governance tool from a VaR-based position limit, and it answers a different question: not 'is today's risk within normal bounds', but 'could a single plausible crisis threaten our survival'. Suppose this firm holds Rs 2 crore of capital and its risk committee has set a rule that no single stress scenario, historical or hypothetical, may imply a loss exceeding 25% of capital, Rs 50,00,000.

stats.label: Stress limit (25% of Rs 2 crore capital)
stats.context: The threshold set by the risk committee

stats.label: GFC loss as share of total capital
stats.context: Under the 25% cap, but not by much

body.text: This portfolio has not technically breached its stress limit, but at 85.5% of the allowed threshold, it is close enough that a well-run framework would flag it for review before it becomes a genuine breach, not after. This is exactly the kind of early warning a purely VaR-based limit, sitting comfortably at Rs 1,39,560 against presumably a much larger daily limit, would never surface.

columns.label: Routine Monitoring, Log and Move On
points: Daily VaR within its usual range, no Basel traffic-light zone concerns
Backtesting exception count consistent with the model's stated confidence level
Stress scenario results well below their assigned limits
Sensitivity figures broadly stable versus the last review

columns.label: Escalation Territory, Risk Committee Conversation
points: Backtesting lands in Basel's Yellow or Red zone, or the Kupiec test rejects the model
A stress scenario result approaches or breaches its assigned capital-based limit
A new position type materially changes the portfolio's sensitivity profile
A scenario in the library no longer reflects current market structure or macro conditions

children.text: Keeping the Framework Alive: Periodic Review

A scenario library assembled once and never revisited quietly goes stale. Markets change structure, new instruments enter a book, and the specific vulnerabilities worth stress testing shift over time. A framework needs its own periodic health check, the same instinct behind backtesting a VaR model, applied to the stress testing process itself.

body.title: Stress Testing Framework Health Check
steps: Does the scenario library still reflect the portfolio's current composition, or have new position types been added since it was last updated?
Are the historical scenarios still the most relevant ones available, or has a new crisis occurred that should be added to the library?
Do the hypothetical scenarios reflect today's macro environment, or are they built around risks that have already receded?
Have stress-test-based limits been reviewed against current capital levels, not just left at their original figures?
Has a reverse stress test been run recently to search for scenarios the existing library has not yet imagined?

body.title: Deciding Whether to Escalate
body.scenario: A desk's risk committee has a stress limit of 25% of capital. This quarter, a newly added hypothetical scenario, built around a sudden RBI rate hike cycle, produces a loss equal to 23% of capital, up from 14% the previous quarter, driven mainly by a large new bond position added over the last two months.
body.prompt: Should this be treated as routine monitoring or escalation territory, and what would you want to know before deciding?
body.modelAnswer: This leans toward escalation territory, not because the limit has been breached, 23% is still under 25%, but because of the trend and its cause. The jump from 14% to 23% in one quarter, clearly traced to a specific new position, is exactly the kind of early signal a good framework is built to catch before an actual breach happens. Before finalizing a decision, check the size and duration of the new bond position relative to the rest of the book, confirm whether the rate hike scenario's assumed magnitude is still appropriate given current RBI policy signals, and ask whether the desk intends to grow this bond position further, since the current trajectory suggests the 25% limit could be breached next quarter without any change in market conditions at all, purely from continued position growth.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What fundamentally distinguishes a stress testing framework from simply running a stress test once?
options: A framework always uses larger shock magnitudes than a one-off test
A framework is recurring and governed, with defined cadence, limits, escalation rules, and periodic review of the scenario library itself
A framework only uses hypothetical scenarios, never historical ones
A framework does not require any VaR or Expected Shortfall calculations
body.explanation: The specific numbers a scenario produces matter less than what happens around them, whether they are checked on a schedule, tied to real limits, escalated when they approach those limits, and revisited as the portfolio and macro environment change. That operating discipline is what separates a framework from a single analysis.

body.text: VaR tells you what an ordinary day costs. Expected Shortfall tells you how bad the tail of an ordinary day gets. Stress testing tells you what a genuine crisis costs. A real risk framework needs all three, running together, on a schedule, with limits that actually trigger action.

points: A stress testing framework is a recurring, governed process, scenario library, cadence, limits, escalation rules, and periodic review, not a single one-time analysis.

Comparing this course's own worked figures side by side, a Rs 1,39,560 daily VaR against a Rs 42,75,000 historical stress loss, makes the case for running both disciplines together rather than relying on VaR alone.
Stress-test-based limits answer a different question than VaR-based limits, whether a single plausible crisis threatens survival, not just whether today's risk sits within a normal range.
Escalation should trigger on trends approaching a limit, not only outright breaches, exactly as the worked example showed a stress result climbing from 14% to 23% of capital in one quarter.

A scenario library, like a VaR model, needs its own periodic health check, refreshed historical scenarios, updated hypothetical scenarios, and regular reverse stress testing to search for what the existing library has not yet imagined.

Across this course: VaR (Chapter 2) measures an ordinary bad day, Expected Shortfall and backtesting (Chapter 3) make that measurement coherent and verified, and stress testing (Chapter 4) covers everything a probability-based model was never built to see. None of the three replaces the other two.
